MR. MORISON-ACCURACY OF TORONTO "STAR" REPORT RESPECTING DELAY OF CHRISTMAS RECESS BY OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this morning on a question of privilege affecting members of the Standing Committee on Regional Development in general and more particularly myself. It was reported in the Toronto Star of December 17 that I had charged that the opposition was delaying the Christmas recess. The report goes on to state that the committee could not adjourn for holidays before dealing with the problems of unemployment as we were trying to do through Bill C-205.
There are some people in this world who have illusions of grandeur, but I should like to assure the House that I am not one of them. I know very well where the power in this House lies, and it certainly does not lie with chairmen of committees.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF STUDY COMMITTEE-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to table in the two official languages the report of the study committee on bankruptcy and insolvency legislation together with two statements being issued herewith.
The report contains proposals for changes and recommends that a new Bankruptcy Act be enacted to deal in a comprehensive way with both commercial and noncommercial bankruptcy. The government, for its part, has examined the report and is in general accord with the recommendations of the committee.
The revision of our bankruptcy and insolvency laws ranks high in the list of priorities. I should like to introduce a bill as soon as possible, and I should therefore appreciate it if interested associations and organizations and the public in general could give me the benefit of their views on the report and their suggestions before the end of January next so that those views can be taken into account in our drafting work.
In conclusion, I want to express the thanks and gratitude of the government to the members of the committee, Messrs. Tasse, Honsberger, Carignan and Landry, for the work they have done in preparing this report.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for providing us with a copy of the report and an indication of his remarks in sufficient time for us to be able to comment with a little more precision on the subject matter.
The report, as we see it, makes an extensive review of bankruptcy legislation as it is applied not only in Canada but elsewhere. It draws attention to the fact that the Parliament of Canada has exclusive legislative power in the field of bankruptcy and insolvency, and that these two subjects have been broadly interpreted by the courts. As the report further comments, in the operation of federal legislation in this area Parliament has come into conflict with the exclusive legislative competence of provincial legislatures, particularly in connection with the administration of justice, property and civil rights and other matters. Some provinces have taken steps to deal with such questions involving insolvency, such as the

I wonder, however, whether the minister is right in asking for comments by the end of January since he intends to bring in legislation at an early date. I suggest to him that because of the vastly changed social and economic conditions it would be better to refer the report to the appropriate committee, say the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, and that the public be invited to make representations and comments with regard to it. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no point in making representations to the minister himself, with the minister then introducing a bill which would have to be commented upon and likely severely attacked and modified in committee. I suggest that in the long run the better procedure would be to refer the report to the committee and have representations made publicly, not to the minister. It is not the minister and his officials who are going to decide the bankruptcy law of this country; the provinces have something to say, as does also the public.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF FISHERIES CLOSING LINES

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of Fisheries and Forestry):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF FISHERIES CLOSING LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by amending the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act earlier this year Parliament laid the foundation for the establishment of exclusive Canadian fishing zones comprising certain areas of the sea adjacent to the coast of Canada. These provisions were enabling only. The creation of new zones requires executive action by way of an Order in Council.
I am pleased to inform the House today that the required action is now being taken to draw "fisheries closing lines" across the entrance to the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the Bay of Fundy, Queen Charlotte Sound and Dixon Entrance-Hecate Strait. A government notice to this effect will be published in the Canada Gazette on December 26, 1970.
The fisheries closing lines will become effective immediately upon the expiration of the mandatory 60 days waiting period imposed by the amended Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act.
The special areas to be enclosed by fisheries closing lines are important fishing zones for Canada. The Gulf of St. Lawrence has had annual landings of up to 550 million pounds of fish valued at $31 million, the Bay of Fundy s landings are about 300 million pounds yearly, worth about $12 million, and the Pacific Coast area has landings of 180 million pounds, worth $37 million.
Having established these new fishing zones, the Canadian government intends to conclude negotiations for the phasing out of the fishing activities of certain countries which have traditionally fished in the areas concerned, namely, the United Kingdom, Denmark, France, Italy, Norway, Portugal and Spain. Canada has recently entered into an agreement on reciprocal fishing
December 18, 1970

Fisheries Closing Lines
privileges with the United States and the activities of United States fishermen in the areas concerned will not be affected by the promulgation of the fisheries closing lines.
Anti-pollution provisions of our Federal Fisheries Act and the Canada Shipping Act will apply within the limits of our new fishing zones, thus adding additional scope to Canada's efforts to preserve and improve the marine environment around our shores.
I would now like to table a four-page statement which was prepared in consultation with the Department of External Affairs. It provides additional information on the promulgation of the fisheries closing lines as defined by the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act. May I ask the permission of the House, Mr. Speaker, to have this statement appended to today's Hansard.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF FISHERIES CLOSING LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
listened with interest to the statement made by the Minister of Fisheries which indicates that action will finally be taken to conserve some of our fisheries resources. I know this announcement will be welcomed by all Canadians, and it will be especially welcomed by fishermen and processors on the east and west coasts.
While waiting for some action on this matter, many of our fishermen were beginning to realize the meaning of the word eternity, for history records that legislation respecting our territorial waters and fisheries laws was introduced by the Hon. Paul Martin, then Secretary of State for External Affairs, with much fanfare back on May 20, 1964. At that time the minister said that the bill respecting the territorial sea and the fishing zones of Canada was not enabling legislation. "On proclamation , he said, "the 12-mile fishing zone will be established- there can be no doubt about this point." A lot of fish have passed over the rails of foreign fishing vessels since that date. Today we see our fisheries resources seriously affected. In fact they have been depleted to the danger level as a result of the inaction and procrastination of this government.
I would point out that the announcement made by the minister today is long overdue, and in our view it is only a beginning. It is only the beginning on the long road back toward obtaining and retaining fishing resources which rightfully belong to our Canadian fishermen. However, I say it is only a beginning since the action taken today will leave many problems still unresolved.
The exclusive fishing zones, for example, as announced by the minister are not complete protection for the stocks of fish on our coasts. The only way to provide for proper conservation is to vest in the coastal states ownership and jurisdiction over the fishery resources on the continental shelf. This would be a logical extension of the United Nations convention on the continental shelf which already recognizes ownership of resources on and under

the sea-bed of the shelf. Even this would not provide protection for anadromous species like salmon which roam far to sea during their early stages. Canada's Atlantic salmon are being intercepted on the high seas of the Atlantic, and the International Commission for the North Atlantic Fishery has expressed grave concern about the depletion of this valuable resource. In our opinion, nothing short of universal acceptance of the abstention principle will adequately protect Canadian salmon on both coasts.
[DOT] (11:30 a.m.)
Finally, this country must do everything within its power to work toward convening another United Nations Law of the Sea Conference at which we must strive for acceptance of at least two principles. One of these principles is the continental shelf concept for our fisheries resources. The other is the universal acceptance of the abstention principle for an anadromous species like salmon. In order to bring this about we need someone in the Department of External Affairs who recognizes the value to Canadians of our fishing industry, as it is obvious that the present minister does not share our concern. In fact, the present minister was only recently in Europe and he made no effort, according to his own statement to me in the House, to resolve the differences which exist between Canada and France over fishing rights surrounding the French-owned islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. In view of the importance of the fishing industry I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will consider strengthening the Department of External Affairs with someone knowledgeable on fisheries matters so that progress can be made at the international level toward solving some of our thorny fishing problems.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my appreciation to the minister for his kindness in sending us a copy of the statement he made earlier so that we could have a look at it. I think it might have been worth while if we could also have had a look at the four-page statement to be appended to Hansard. It would have made his statement more meaningful because the statement the minister made is sufficiently bare to leave a few gaps in our understanding of what has taken place. I believe it also indicates that we cannot have a great deal of faith in what the minister and the government say concerning fisheries matters because when the bill to amend the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act was before the standing committee during the last session the minister said that in a matter of a few days he would have the fisheries closing lines established, but those few days have dragged on into seven months. That does not lead us to have much faith in the pronouncements of the minister about what he intends to do but indicates that we should pay more attention to what he does or does not do.
One point that has been dealt with extensively before the committee and in fishing circles, a matter with which we have concerned ourselves for some time, is the extension of our jurisdiction to the continental shelf and continental slope. The minister himself made a great play on that idea before the committee and elsewhere, saying
December 18, 1970

that it was the intention of the government to extend jurisdiction to those areas so as to include groundfish as well to the extent we would have jurisdiction over it and to prosecute the fishery to the full extent on continental slope.
A few years ago the committee on fisheries which examined the estimates unanimously recommended to the government that the fisheries jurisdiction of Canada be extended to the continental shelf and slope. This has been completely ignored by the minister in his statement today and up to this time. There is no indication in the statement that any consideration is being given to that matter. In fact, its phraseology in terms of drawing fisheries closing lines across the entrances to certain waters indicates to me that this matter has in fact been completely ignored.
In dealing with fisheries we must concern ourselves with two fronts: first, the extent to which we can extend our jurisdiction to the edge of the continental slope and, second, the extent to which we can involve ourselves in international agreements with other nations to ensure that the fish of the high seas which originate in our land are preserved to the fishermen of this nation. We have a potential lever which was not used. If the government had taken the action of extending the fisheries closing lines out to the continental shelf and the edge of the continental slope, we might have been able to prevent the minister giving the right to the Soviet Union to fish inside our territorial sea, as he did earlier this year.
To return to the point I made about the degree of faith we should have in the minister, when he was asked in the House about the agreement with the Soviet Union he said he would gladly refer that matter to the standing committee. So far he has forgotten about that as well. I think we need a little more action and concern not only on the part of the Department of Fisheries but also on the part of the Department of External Affairs, and less froth and foam.

ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMPROVEMENT OF SATURDAY WICKET SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that main post offices and most postal stations in urban centres will return to complete counter service on Saturdays.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMPROVEMENT OF SATURDAY WICKET SERVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMPROVEMENT OF SATURDAY WICKET SERVICE
speechtext:
This is to replace the limited service offered since the start of five-day week letter carrier delivery in February 1969.
Extensive surveys were taken of the services provided on Saturdays, and these have shown a need to make services such as stamps and money orders available again at the majority of offices studied. However, the surveys also indicated that the need varies widely from city to city and even in different sections of some cities.

The hours of Saturday service at individual offices and the selection of locations to provide the increased service will, therefore, be determined by community needs. This will be left to the discretion of senior field managers who are familiar with local conditions and service demands. The improved service will begin on a regular basis from January 9, 1971. A Merry Christmas to all Post Office employees and to all customers of the Post Office.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by thanking the minister for his courtesy in providing, in good time and in both languages, copies of his statement. Indeed, I would say to him that his general considerateness and courtesy have detracted somewhat from the spice and enjoyment of the role I am trying to perform on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party.
I am impressed by the strangeness of the fact that it has become necessary to announce in the House of Commons a resumption of postal service to the Canadian people. I appreciate the fact that it is being done but it is surprising that it was necessary that such an announcement be made. I think, Sir, that this action marks another repudiation of the more preposterous and tortuous innovations of the minister's predecessor, and I commend this minister for his willingness to recognize that certain events, incidents and developments of some months ago were in fact very bad mistakes.
[DOT] (11:40 a.m.)
I note that it required "extensive surveys of the services provided on Saturday." This, I thought, would hardly have been necessary. No major inquiry should have been required because hosts of Canadians do have difficulty in transacting business with the Post Office on days other than Saturday, and many Canadians combine a visit to the Post Office with their Saturday shopping. I think it was not required to have a massive inquiry into that.

I am a little concerned also about the suggestion of flexibility. It seems to me that there is now too much variation in the postal service. Rural Canadians get six-day delivery, urban Canadians get five-day delivery, and there are many Canadians in suburban areas who are not quite sure where they stand or where the postman is going to come from and on what day.
As I said at the beginning, I commend the minister for taking this remedial action, but I say to him that it will not be sufficient. The five-day mail service has been a fiasco, and the sooner we get back to six-day mail service, which most countries in the world have, the better it will be for all, including those in the Post Office. Much of the delay in the mail delivery in Canada-and it has been appalling in the last few years-stems from this lost weekend, this blackout of mail delivery from Friday until Monday, which is followed by a backlog of mail that has to be worked through on Monday, and the delays sometimes last until Wednesday. This is not my normal day in the House, Mr. Speaker, but it may be the last occasion before the festive season or before the recess when I can make a statement on motions. I welcome this opportunity to report briefly regarding a matter of interest to all members of the House. It concerns the collective bargaining currently in process between the railways and certain unions representing some of the employees of the railways.
As members are aware, some time ago I announced the appointment of what I described as industry specialists to assist in the process of minimizing industrial unrest and, more particularly, to assist in obtaining collective agreements prior to the expiry date of existing contracts. Hon. members may recall that this approach resulted in an early settlement in the railway industry in 1968.
I am pleased, therefore, to announce that it can be safely stated that the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway will sign within the hour a memorandum of settlement with unions representing some 20,000 shopcraft employees. This constitutes, if ratified, a settlement ten days before the present contract expires.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
In conclusion, I would like, therefore, Mr. Speaker, to pay tribute not only to the representatives of the unions and the companies but also to our industry specialist, Mr. Arthur Gibbons, and my director of conciliation and arbitration, Mr. William Kelly, who have worked very closely with the parties for several weeks. In my opinion, both Mr. Kelly and Mr. Gibbons remind us of the fact that our public servants rank with the best in any country.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SETTLEMENT OF CONTRACT NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN RAILWAY SHOPCRAFT EMPLOYEES AND EMPLOYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say a word or two in response to the welcome announcement just made by the Minister of Labour. We are glad to learn that a settlement has been reached and that the signing of it is in prospect today between Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway on the one hand and representatives of the shopcraft unions on the other. I have no objection to the minister taking credit for his department for the good job that has been done. It is a good job for the industry and a good job for Canada.
There is just one point I should like to make, Mr. Speaker. If my information is correct, the issue of pensions was not on the table, at least toward the end of these negotiations, and that is probably one of the reasons why it has been possible to reach agreement. I suggest to the minister that as far as the other railway unions are concerned there is a good deal more anxiety over the pension issue and that settlement in those cases may not be possible within the forseeable future.
Business of the House
I therefore urge the minister to do everything that he can on the issue of pensions. In particular I urge that he make available these good offices that he has spoken of, and his own good offices, to his colleague, the Minister of Transport, to get Canadian National Railways to realize that if they would comply with the unanimous wish of this House of Commons concerning pension increases the whole issue would be settled a lot sooner and we would have peace in the railway industry.
This is a terribly important part of the whole railway issue, and it is not good enough for the government not to get involved in it. The Minister of Transport is a good man but he needs help, and I urge the Minister of Labour to give him that help so that this issue can be settled, preferably before Christmas.

That Bill C-205, to amend the Regional Development Incentives Act, be amended in Clause 3 by adding to subsection 4 of section 5 the following:
provided however that any incentive shall be granted only after the applicant has provided the Crown or its designated agency with such number of shares in the application firm that the Minister considers to be equivalent in value to the incentive except that where the amount of the incentive is less than one million dollars the Minister may grant an exemption to this provision.
When Bill C-205 was presented to the House for second reading, Mr. Speaker, members of this party agreed to second reading of the bill in order that its provisions and its implications could be studied further in the committee. We agreed also because we were anxious to help in any way in order that the regional development program could be extended or used usefully in dealing with some of the problems facing Canada. At that time we made it quite clear that we felt the provisions of the bill were inadequate in terms of fulfilling the objectives of it as stated by the minister and the government.

December 18, 1970

We also had serious misgivings about the bill because we felt it jeopardized the principles of a regional development program, and that in fact it might create some serious problems for the future of such programs. Now that we have gone through the committee stage and have had a chance to question the minister as well as hear witnesses who are experts in the field of regional development, we have to say that this is poor legislation. I suggest that the bill before us at the present time will emasculate the regional development program.
At the committee we heard from the minister and the deputy minister regarding this bill. They did not present an opening statement, they simply said they would answer any questions we had. That is a rather unusual procedure, one which I find is becoming too common on the part of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). The minister and the deputy minister simply took the attitude: We are alright, Jack; everything is fine. Just leave it to us and we will see that everything is fixed up.
This was not good enough, Mr. Speaker, and we heard from a number of witnesses. We heard from representatives of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council and the Canadian Council of Rural Development. We heard from Professor Tom Brewis, probably the outstanding authority on regional development programs and policies in Canada. This witness made it quite clear that this bill would scuttle the regional development program. Every one of the witness presented serious criticisms of Bill C-205; and this is a very serious matter, all of them expressed a growing disillusionment with the government's regional development programs as they have been brought forward to the present time.
Then, we heard from the minister and the deputy minister again but they had the same approach. We had to pry information from them. They refused to prepare a considered reply to the representations that had been made by the various expert witnesses who came before the committee. At one point the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion tried to slough off some of the evidence that had been presented by indicating that these were just words of a professor, why should we worry about them? I think it is a very serious matter when the minister refuses to give serious consideration to the points of criticism presented not only by members of the House and members of the Regional Development Committee, but also by some of the expert witnesses who appeared before that committee.
As a matter of fact, the minister and the deputy did not even consider it important enough to have a person there to monitor the evidence presented by the witnesses. They were not in position to reply to some of the points raised earlier in the evidence. I should state that the Parliamentary Secretary to the minister was present. He was very attentive and took part in the proceedings. I was pleased with that part of the performance at least. The minister and the deputy were not in a position to adequately answer the points presented to members of the committee. They were not in a position to adequately answer the criticisms and questions put forward by mem-
Regional Development Incentives Act
bers when they came before the committee the second time.
Consequently, we moved a number of amendments at the committee stage of the proceedings. Most of them were designed to make the best possible bill out of a poor piece of legislation. We at least tried to make it more workable by giving the legislation before us some focus and direction in order that it might be based on some sort of sound principles of regional development. All of these amendments were summarily rejected by the Liberal majority on the committee. I suggest one reason they rejected them all is that most of those members were absent for the testimony of the witnesses. They did not consider the evidence important enough to stay and hear it being presented by representatives of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, the Canadian Council of Rural Development and Professor Brewis. Most of them attended only when they thought their presence was needed to rubberstamp the government's legislation. When amendments were moved by opposition members they would say "no" before the amendments were even read.

The hon. member was one of those who took part in the proceedings and he knows very well that is true. The only thing he could do was make noise, such as he is making right now. I suggest the performance of most of the Liberal members of this committee was disgraceful. They performed a poor service for their constituents and the people of Canada in the way they conducted themselves during the committee proceedings this week.
Today, we are moving one amendment which would make a major difference to this legislation. It would change the direction of the government's programs and the direction in which it is trying to take this legislation with Bill C-205. The amendment which has just been presented to the House provides for public equity in undertakings where there is substantial assistance provided by the people of Canada for new developments.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
The amendment which has been moved contemplates a Canada Development Corporation. The government said it would introduce this legislation at this session. When it will come forward is difficult to say at the present time. The government has given no indication. Possibly it will be one of the never-never things for which this government has become rather well known. "Never-never" certainly can be applied to its policies in respect of a Canada Development Corporation. The amendment before us, together with other complementary developments such as the formation of the Canada Development Corporation, would assist in planning a comprehensive

December 18, 1970
Regional Development Incentives Act approach to regional development. It would also stop the give-aways to large corporations which I suggest is one serious feature in respect of the government's programs as we have them at the present time. It would assist in the process of helping to regain control over the Canadian economy. We must start now and not wait for some manana which may never come. I think it is clear that the government's regional development program is getting into a worse morass every day. This legislation will be the final blow and that is the reason we believe it must be given very close scrutiny and study by the House. It will destroy the program as a regional development program.
As I indicated at second reading, we were prepared to give further consideration to the bill in committee. We were particularly sympathetic to the proposition, which was the government's contention, that this legislation was a key portion of the government's program for Quebec in dealing with problems with which all hon. members are familiar. In the committee we found that it will do nothing of the sort. Every witness pointed out that this program will not be of immediate help to Montreal and other areas of Quebec. We also pointed out that regional economic programs are no substitute for an effective national economic policy. Every witness before the committee pointed out that there is a considerable time lag in the program between its commencement and the implementation and impact of it. It must be considered as a long-run program. This is borne out by the evidence that up to this week only $3.4 million in incentives have been paid out. Let us contrast that with the total amount of offers which had been made under the Regional Development Incentives Act to the end of October, the latest month for which I have a compilation available. Up to October 31, offers had been made under the Regional Development Incentives Act of approximately $102 million. The figure to the end of November of course would be somewhat higher. But only $3.4 million has actually been paid out.
I acknowledge of course that as a result of some of the offers which have been made, but which have not yet been paid out, some work is under way. Certainly, that is an obvious fact. The basic point remains, however, that there is a significant and important time lag in these programs. They must be considered on a longer run basis and as long-run programs. The minister admitted that this legislation would do nothing for Montreal and Quebec this winter. He has admitted that we might as well write off this program in terms of it having any impact during the current winter. I suggest that the minister has performed a disservice to his own province by some of the statements he made before the committee. I think all of us will acknowledge the problems which exist in Quebec, as well as the various problems which exist in other parts of Canada. But the minister seems to have developed a habit of making very strong statements in order to back up his very weak arguments. I think we have had several examples of this over the past few months. It would seem that we have had a further example in some of the statements made by the minister before the committee in which he tried to paint a very
drastic picture of the situation in Quebec and thereby once again exaggerate the problem.
I believe it has been properly said that the finance minister of Quebec could not let these comments pass, even though he is a colleague of the minister in political terms. I should like to quote from the Montreal Gazette of December 16. This is an article headed "Marchand exaggerated-Garneau". The article reads as follows:
Finance Minister Raymond Garneau said yesterday he disagrees with a suggestion by Jean Marchand, federal minister of regional economic expansion, that Quebec's economy is likely to collapse if investment in Montreal does not improve drastically in the next three years.
Mr. Garneau told a news conference he is happy with the federal government's decision to make the Montreal region eligible for economic incentives, but said Mr. Marchand exaggerated when he predicted the province's economy could collapse.
The federal minister made his comments Monday during a meeting of the Commons regional expansion committee examining proposed amendments to the Regional Development Incentives Act.
The amendments would make the Montreal area eligible for a special incentives program until Dec. 31, 1973.
"If nothing happens before 1973 I don't know what problem we would have left to solve," Mr. Marchand said.

speechtext:
When one o'clock was called I was making reference to the regular flaps that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) seems to get into, his most recent one being with respect to this bill. He seems to be in a panic to do something, to do anything, it would seem, to try to find something that would at least appear to be a solution to some of the problems that he and others have allowed to develop for some time. So, he insists on rushing this legislation through the House at the last minute, legislation which is admitted by all parties in the House to be very important.
I would like to draw to the attention of the minister some of his previous statements when the Regional Development Incentives Act was originally introduced in the House. He indicated at that time that this bill had to be rushed through, the government needed it right away. But then he agreed we must never do this sort of thing again. Now, we are on the same old merry-go-round again.
I should like to examine the amendment which I moved on behalf of the New Democratic Party in relation


December 18, 1970
to the bill before us. I think it must be examined in the light of the operation of the program which is being carried out under the authority of the Regional Development Incentives Act. The first major objection to the bill is that it is being used to accomplish national economic objectives, something for which the program and the legislation were never designed. This was expressed very lucidly by Professor Brewis when he appeared before the committee. Professor Brewis pointed out to the Regional Development Committee at its meeting last Tuesday:
The bill leaves me with a feeling of considerable uneasiness, and as I have listened to the discussion today, I must say that my uneasiness has increased. The bill introduces what seems to be a major reorientation of policy in the direction of measures to reduce cyclical unemployment rather than measures to improve the long run economic potential of the less favoured regions of the country.
Then, he went on to say that he wanted to remind the minister of what the latter said in a speech in Halifax in October of 1968. This is what the minister had to say on that occasion:
I believe that in our business, the sensible effective action will be found in the middle area between short run expedience and vague long run plans.
The minister then suggested that 15 years was a reasonable time horizon on which to do the planning. He emphasized that his first principle was as follows:
We will not offer short run expediency or long run vagueness. Measures must not be selected just because they catch up problems for the moment.
Then, Professor Brewis went on to comment:
I think it is a great pity that the minister did not stick to his guns.
When Professor Brewis appeared before the committee he had some other relevant comments to make with regard to this particular point. He said that the nature of the incentives is not such as to ameliorate significantly the lot of the unemployed in the short run, and from past experience it seems more likely to benefit a large number of companies. Professor Brewis said that with regard to the short run, in his budget speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) speaking of important amendments to the Regional Development Incentives Act, said:
It is also very difficult to predict the volume of investment likely to be effective or the probable cost of the incentives. Judging from experience with the program to date, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion foresees a total increase in outlays because of the new program amounting to about $130 million over the period of the next few years.
[DOT] (2.10 p.m.)
That is the end of the quotation from the budget speech of the Minister of Finance. Professor Brewis went on to say:
If we take Mr. Benson's figure of $130 million and assume in the light of past experience (according to DREE estimates) that $5,000 of incentives creates one job then these incentives may create 25,000-30,000 jobs. Since there are currently between 600,000 and 700,000 unemployed, this will result in one man out of 20 getting a job. For this marginal result a massive change in the DREE legislation is envisaged.

Mr. Speaker, I think I can assure you that my remaining remarks will be pertinent to the amendment before the House. I wish to deal with the growth centre concept and to relate this to the amendment. Wb are calling for a degree of public participation in regional development incentives programs and feel that the public should be provided with a share of the companies being assisted through those programs. In this regard, it is very important to note that the government's original concept, which it developed in this program for growth centres, is in disarray. The adoption of this amendment would help to give the program some better direction and focus. The minister has stated that the special areas had provided some element of growth centres, but nevertheless he hedged and did not want to become too specific.
If we are to develop a growth centre concept and follow it through, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that rather than undertaking programs on an ad hoc basis where you simply consider applications from a widespread area which has been designated by regulation as authorized

under the legislation, the government could help to give some better directions to its programs and some better focussing on this important matter.
This point was stressed by witnesses before the committee, particularly those from the Atlantic provinces Economic Council, who showed that there was considerable confusion in the government's programs. They did not know whether the growth centre concept was being followed and whether it was still one of the objectives of the department. They pointed out the number of problems developing within the Atlantic provinces as a result of the present pattern of dispersal of grants.

Mr. Speaker, I am suggesting it is quite relevant to follow the growth centre concept in the department's proposals, and to involve the public and the government in by requiring that the government receive a portion of the ownership of these companies. It is hoped that when companies receive these grants, they will help to carry through the objectives of the department, objectives which it has stated in the past. There is some confusion at present as to whether these companies are fulfilling these objectives.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
I should like to pass on to the next point that I wanted to raise, which I feel is the most important one in connection with the amendment before the House. This point relates to the government's reliance on private enterprise and its large giveaways to corporations. This I feel is one of the most damning features of the government's implementation and administration of this act, and it is one of the major reasons why we have introduced this amendment. A large proportion of the funds which are being committed by this department are in the form of large giveaways to corporations. In the cases where this is simply a giveaway grant, in which there is for a limited period control over the firm receiving the grant, the grant becomes ineffective in terms of the public control of the investment after that time. This matter is too important to be simply left in the hands of private enterprise. The entire development of our regional development program is too important for that. We simply cannot leave it in the hands of private enterprise. Because of the very nature of the problem and the very nature of the solutions, we cannot leave it to private enterprise.
Our regional development problems and regional disparities in Canada stem from the fact that we have allowed so much of our development to take place in the past as a result of a form of giveaways. We have allowed private enterprise to do whatever it wanted, regardless of whether it met the needs of the people of Canada or whether its actions benefited the people of Canada. The size of this program is illustrated by the pattern of grants
December 18, 1970

which have been made by the federal government or which at least have been committed by the federal government at the present time.
I have an analysis before me of grants which were committed by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion under this act up to the end of September. The analysis shows that the ten largest grants totalled some $48,750,000, out of a total for all grants of $83,168,000. This means that 58.6 per cent of those grants totalled $1 million or over. That is the dividing line provided in the amendment I have moved, Mr. Speaker. It proposes that there be a public sharing in any grant of $1 million or over. These ten companies, as a result of these grants, will provide some 3,309 new jobs out of a total of 14,015 which it is stated will be created by the end of September. That is 23.6 per cent of the jobs which it is suggested will be so created. And that percentage of jobs will result from 58.6 per cent of the grants. These ten companies include Sydney Steel, which is a public corporation, Ecstall Mining IBM, Control Data, McCain Foods, Becan-court Glass, F.W. Pine, C.I.P. Homekakers, T.S. Simms & Company and Askland Chemicals. It will be noted, of course, that Sydney Steel is, as I have mentioned, a public corporation, and that therefore it should be and could be quite validly excluded from this particular pattern. I have done this as well.
If the figures concerning Sydney Steel are excluded, it will be shown that the nine remaining companies will receive about $32,866,000 in grants, or 48.8 per cent of the commitments for grants made to the end of September, the total being $67,284,000. Compare that with the 23.6 per cent of employment out of the total employment to be created through this program, and it will still be shown that there is quite a vast disparity.
These grants are being provided to large corporations; in some cases, they are foreign-owned corporations as well. We feel that the programs could be much better directed if a share in the ownership of these plants were vested in the Crown. I think it should be noted as well that this amendment contemplates the creation of the Canada Development Corporation.
It will be noted from the wording of my amendment that I suggest that the shares in any such enterprise should be vested either in the Crown or its designated agency. Without naming that agency in the amendment, we had it in our minds that the Canada Development Corporation could be and should be that agency.
It seems to me that one of the criticisms of this program is this: there has been an ad hoc pattern of development that has come about simply through the process of responding to applications from firms located in widely spread out designated areas and allowing those firms to decide, on the basis of their own narrow interest, as to whether a plant would be commenced.
A further aspect of this entire program has to do with the grants to foreign-owned and foreign-controlled corporations. It has already been noted that up to the end of 1969, under the various incentives programs, incentive grants were made by the government. They were made
Regional Development Incentives Act under various programs, including old programs now being terminated, and they were made to foreign controlled corporations. These, I suggest, could be controlled more adequately as a result of the amendment that I have moved. There is certainly no indication that there has been any change in the pattern of grants which have been offered under the Regional Development Incentives Act.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we must ask this question: where is the government going with respect to the question of foreign ownership? Certainly the government has indicated that it has directed a statement of policy to be prepared. Just when that will be available is difficult to tell. I am not too hopeful of the final result, especially when one considers the manner in which the department is currently contributing to the further giveaway and sellout of the Canadian economy as a result of grants being provided under this program. I think this is a very serious matter, Mr. Speaker, because the minister must take the prime responsibility for the destruction of his program. You know, he entered the government as one of the three wise men. It seems to me that something happened on the road to Damascus; or, one might say, something funny happened on the way to the forum. We moved an amendment in committee. We had some difficulty getting our point across. However, I think we did make our point. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not have the privilege of being a member of this committee. I would have liked to have heard the discussion. I have tried to read the proceedings in the committee reports, but I have not had too much success. I would have liked to have seen some amendments introduced at the report stage as a result of those discussions.
We have before us a specific resolution which goes a long way towards solving the problem which, according to the evidence, is the major criticism of Bill C-205. This criticism relates to the almost total coverage of Canada by incentive programs. If there are one or two more amendments, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will be involved in every industrial development in Canada. If that is necessary, it is a sad commentary. It does not meet the hopes and aspirations we had for this legislation.
It is generally agreed that when a number of areas are designated, some consideration is given to incentives in slow growth areas. In fact, we must draw these areas to
the attention of those wishing to establish industries. If the city of Montreal, with the largest population of any center of Canada, is designated, this will not help the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Hopkins) who last year made a very strong plea to have his area designated. I do not have much hope that my area in northern Ontario will be designated, something for which I have fought for two or three years.

speechtext: Order, please. I know that the hon. member is very experienced and is familiar with the rules of this House. I wonder if he would now come to the amendment. There has been quite a bit of latitude. There will also be the third reading stage.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
I thank Your Honour for inviting me to make a speech on third reading. I am from an area which has not received much consideration in the past. This proliferation of designations will not really help. Of the moneys that have been spent, 66 per cent has gone to foreign owned companies, most of them branch plants processing the raw materials of this country. If it had not been for the incentives that were offered, they probably would not have located in those areas.
This amendment provides that in areas when industry will not locate unless there is a very large incentive, we should attach a condition to the contribution we make that the government will receive equity shares. I am sure that many members of my party have already, or will shortly, reach that conclusion. I am sure other hon. members agree that we have to give consideration to the total ownership of specific industries in specific areas. We are going to have to direct our money into specific areas in order to provide employment in those areas at the lowest cost.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
To give one example, we are providing a million dollars of federal money to one company. This program began on the basis of the number of unemployed in an area, the rate of growth of that area as compared with others, and so on. That million dollars meant the creation of 56 jobs, so these jobs were provided at a cost of $21,000 each. If we are thinking about employment, $21,000 related to 2,000 hours works out at approximately $10,000. This is the contribution we have made. Surely, we are interested in a longer term proposition?
It is almost universally the case that companies which locate in areas they would not normally enter do so because of the incentive carrot which is held out to them. They are not likely to be sure-fire enterprises; many are in serious difficulties before they start, and the grant made by the government strengthens their financial position. Many countries which have been using government direction and inducements to establish industry in particular patterns realize they will not necessarily be viable. When money is put into them they are obviously taking a chance. It is true the companies must meet certain criteria before they are considered worthy of support.

December 18, 1970

Bearing this in mind, I do not think it is at all unreasonable for us to ask for a share of the equity capital in these companies. Then, if they are successful, the people of Canada will make a profit. If they fail, at least we have sought to make a contribution to improving the economy of an area. Some of the companies interested in resource development are in a sound position. I should like to mention one industry in which we have an interest, Polymer Corporation. At one time, nobody wanted to put any money in that undertaking. None of the other companies was interested. But when we needed a substitute for rubber to help the war effort, we established the corporation on a sound basis. It was successful, and every year part of the money spent on it is returned to the Canadian treasury. This is as it should be. If that company had failed, it would have failed in an endeavour which was of great importance to Canada, and we would have been willing to accept the loss. This being so, I can see nothing wrong with our having some say in the development of companies which we are assisting.
Let us consider some of the propositions which were handled by the estates set-up in the Maritime provinces. The board established an interest in some of these companies, participated in financial decisions and exercised a limited degree of control. Obviously, when a company is induced to locate where it would not otherwise locate, it is acting artificially and in these circumstances it will often be difficult to make a success of the venture. In my view, those who have been involved in the regional development program, not only under the existing act but under the two or three measures which preceded it, are to be congratulated on producing as many winners as they have. In supporting this amendment, I suggest the Canadian public should have an opportunity to share in both the successes and the failures of this program. Together with share capital equal to the amount of the incentives grant, they would be able to exercise some degree of control over what is happening. I am concerned about some of the companies which, to my knowledge, have gone into the Maritimes with special support. One of them is a large, multi-national operation whose advantage it is to look at the overall picture. If there is insufficient profit coming from one region, the most paying course is to take the grant and get out. One company has done just that. If we had equity capital in these companies we would find ourselves in a much better position to advise or to cajole or even to ensure a greater degree of success by adding more money if necessary.
In the years ahead, depending on the kind of governments in power, the Canadian people will be bound to participate in industrial development projects to a greater or a lesser extent. Decisions will have to be made by government in the next 20 years whether or not to direct industry into specific areas. If the minister listens to the advice he gets from the provinces, he will find that in their view there is scarcely an area of any province which is not entitled to assistance. Nevertheless, the minister has an obligation under the act not to expand this program to the extent that it becomes unsuccessful. After he has specified the areas to be designated, money will
Regional Development Incentives Act have to flow into the new ventures which are established and in these circumstances it seems to me the government ought surely to be in a position to exercise a degree of control.
There are many ways in which control can be exercised. There is the kind of control Parliament exercises over the CNR which seems to me little more than picking up the tab, most of the time. We control various other government corporations in different ways. It seems to me that when it comes to companies, capitalization is really the basis of the control. We all read the financial papers and note the jockeying which is done for control of a company on the basis of, say, a 20 per cent control of the stock. In my opinion, we should consolidate our assistance in specific areas and obtain some degree of control. In the case of some companies which, to my knowledge, have asked for assistance of the kind the minister can offer, they are unable to borrow funds from the banks or raise them on the open market or extend their operations through the issuing of shares, so they would be very happy to take in the federal government as a partner.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The company would have to make some accounting to, for example, a deputy minister, and in this way the government would exercise some control and evaluation of the operation. In the case of a company like, say, Texas Gulf, it is my guess that such a company would not ask for an incentive grant if this meant they had to provide share capital. They would not want their operation diluted by the federal government sharing in the financial structure, and therefore would not apply for a grant. They would not need to apply because their ability to raise capital is better than that of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). I am sure they would be more successful in floating stock than the federal government. However, if they did apply under the program, I can see no legitimate reason for them to do so, either from a socialist point of view or from the point of view of the most conservative free enterpriser. The previous speaker in the debate is, in my opinion, a pseudo free enterpriser, as I am sure he would agree, yet he is not in favour of this amendment. This shows that he does not really believe in free enterprise.
All we are suggesting in this amendment is that there be another partner in a free enterprise operation. We are not suggesting that the government exercise any undue control that they do not exercise over other companies. All we are suggesting is that they receive equity capital equivalent to the amount they put into the company in question, and that they be allowed to act in the same way as any other shareholder would act. I see no legitimate reason for not taking this first step.
The original incentive program has been a failure, as we are all aware. It is a failure in its total concept, not in individual instances. My colleague mentioned the McCain firm. In my opinion this is a case falling almost outside the incentive program, yet they received assistance. As a

December 18, 1970
Division
result of this assistance a new section was added to their large plant, thus allowing production to take place in Canada. In my opinion, that operation was worthwhile and was a success.
However, as far as ending unemployment is concerned, which was what the program was originally designed to do, it has not been of much help. A limited number of jobs have been created. The capitalization of these jobs has been very high in total, and to that extent has not been successful. I am sure that the minister will agree- indeed he has said this many times-that when you make a program too wide your chance of success becomes less and less with each expansion.
For the program to be successful now, we must rapidly increase over the next year the amount of money that is available. I am sure that the people of this country will be willing to assist through taxation, and to that extent will participate in the program. But surely the public can participate not only in the losses but in the profits in cases where profits are made on their investments. If companies under the program were fair with the government they would be willing to pay a dividend on investments for the lifetime of the investments. If they have been unable to get money elsewhere and turn to the federal government for assistance, surely they should regard equity capital from the government as no different from equity capital from other sources.
I am not an expert on financial matters, and I do not know how many of the companies we have already assisted would agree to the proposal now before the House. But in view of the number of companies that we have supported, it seems to me that this proposition is a very minimal requirement.

In so doing, Mr. Speaker, we shall be registering our grave concern about the course that the government has insisted on following. They have adopted this regional development program with its ramifications, a 15-year program designed to change the structure of areas such as the Atlantic provinces-and you cannot do that overnight-in an attempt to make up for the deficiencies of many years. They have taken this program and used it to meet a short-term, cyclical situation. In so doing they have diluted the bill to the point that it is practically useless to the peripheral areas of this country.
We are fully aware of the seriousness of the situation in Montreal. We are equally aware of the seriousness of the situation throughout the country which is the direct consequence of the government's monetary and fiscal policies in fighting inflation and the deliberate creation of high unemployment.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
We know that this is a very serious matter, but we are concerned about the way the government is attempting to cope with it. We are very concerned that they will take the Regional Development Incentives Act, the main thrust of the government's regional development policy, and use it to meet a situation which by its very nature must be short-term. The excessively high unemployment in Montreal and in most of the industrial areas of the country is short-term; it will pass. The problems in the Atlantic provinces are anything but short-term. The problems in northern Ontario, in eastern Quebec or in some parts of the Prairies are anything but short-term and will require a long-term approach.
The minister has gone full circle; he has gone completely against the assurance that he gave in Halifax in October, 1968. I think his assurance is worth repeating for the record. The minister said:
I believe that in our business the sensible, effective action will be found in the middle area between short-run expedients and vague long-run plans. I propose to choose 15 years as the reasonable time horizon for which we should do our planning-
Nobody quarrelled with that statement at the time, because everybody realized the importance of time and that what the minister was trying to do could not be accomplished over-night. You could not do away with the injustices of a hundred years in a short time. The minister continued as follows:
So let me emphasize my first principle. It is that we won't offer short-run expediency or long-run vagueness. We want to have constructive, practical, medium-length plans. We are going to plan for every possible effort for 15 years.
By the amendments to the bill now before the House the minister has changed the whole concept. Professor Brewis, considered to be one of the experts in Canada on regional development, believes that the minister has reoriented the whole policy by using this program to combat cyclical unemployment. Mr. Speaker, we feel
that the broad ramifications of the minister's actions will be felt for a long time in the regionally disadvantaged areas of this country. That is why we are concerned, and that is why the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council is concerned. In a recent "Newsletter" the council stated:
With so much of the industrial heartland of Canada now eligible for grants, the Atlantic region may well ask what chance it has to compete for new industry. When everything is designated, nothing is designated.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
In our view, that is the main objection to the course the government is following. They have weakened this bill so far as areas like the Atlantic provinces are concerned to the point where it will be virtually impossible, notwithstanding the added incentives, to attract industry because industry will be unable to resist the pull of Montreal, the metropolis of Canada, located right in the major markets of the country. This act was designed in the first place to do just the opposite. It was originally designed to enable areas such as the Atlantic provinces to compete with industrial areas such as Montreal.
Representatives of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council gave evidence before the committee expressing the same reservations in much broader terms, as outlined in their "Newsletter" of December, 1970. They questioned the effectiveness of the program and the ability of the government to administer it now that the proposed amendments would broaden its scope to the extent where practically half the population of the country is involved in the Regional Development Incentives Act.
We should take a long look at this program, Mr. Speaker. We in this party intend to monitor its operation and the power the minister will have under this measure. We shall watch very carefully to ensure that there is consultation, for example, we will be very anxious to see what happens in Quebec and in Montreal, because we believe that this program will not be effective in meeting the immediate need of Montreal, which is jobs. These jobs are needed now, this winter. We question whether this program will meet that need.
During the course of the committee meetings on clause by clause study of this bill, and as a direct consequence of the evidence produced, we were concerned about the wide, discretionary powers enjoyed by the minister. We tried to put forward an amendment which would ensure that the minister used this wide discretionary power only after full consultation-

-with the provinces and the municipalities. We were shocked to learn during the committee stage of the bill that the Atlantic Provinces Advisory Council, which is charged by statute with advising the minister, had not been consulted by the minister since last January.

We expected the minister to live up to the statutory obligation placed upon him by the act and consult the Atlantic Provinces Advisory Council about the formulation of the philosophy that brought about this amendment. I am sure that if he had consulted the advisory council they would have advised him against using this particular measure to combat unemployment in Montreal and southeastern Ontario. They would have advised him against this course because of the consequences it would have upon areas such as the Atlantic provinces.
We were equally disturbed after listening to the presentation of the members of the Rural Development Council, for which the minister also has statutory responsibility. They, too, indicated under questioning that the minister had not consulted them. The minister had not bothered to consult them, yet that body contains on its executive committee Professor Brewis, who, on the subject of regional development, is one of the most knowledgeable scholars in Canada.

Also, the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, that quasi-official body operating in the Atlantic provinces under the patronage of the four Atlantic governments, had not been consulted by this minister. We find it difficult to understand where the minister obtains his advice. Where is he obtaining it? He has yet to tell us. When replying to our direct questions in this regard, he pooh-poohs all our suggestions. He says in so many words, "This is just so much economic theory. You and others have one view; I have my own view." Apparently everybody in Canada is out of step except the minister and his deputy. Unfortunately, in a situation such as this the consequences of that attitude can be serious.
Our amendment would have made it mandatory for the minister to set up an advisory council. We set out in our amendment the composition of that council. We suggested that the council should in part be composed of one nominee from each of the ten provinces, because all ten provinces are now concerned in this program. There are ample precedents for that position. We set out the precedent under the manpower act, a measure for which the minister had some responsibility. We set out the precedent under the Expo act and under the Devco act, for which the minister now has responsibility. There is ample precedent for the Lieutenant Governors in council to make appointments to federal advisory boards.
We stipulated that the board should be comprised of 15 members nominated by the government and a member nominated by each of the ten provinces. This board would have ensured consultation. It was to concern itself with the type of situation now developing in Canada with so much of the country designated. Now provincial governments such as the government of Saskatchewan and perhaps the government of Manitoba, are beginning to designate their own areas. They are doing so because areas in those provinces which have not been included as federally designated areas are at such a disadvantage
Regional Development Incentives Act that the provincial governments have been forced to move in and provide some incentives. Just about the whole country is designated, so what was formerly a regional development policy which gave us some hope has now been translated into a national economic program. The consequences of the government's action, in my view, could be most drastic for areas such as the Atlantic provinces.
The government agreed to accept a watered-down version of our amendment. Imbued with the spirit of Christmas and the spirit of compromise, they agreed that it was necessary to hold consultations. They agreed it was essential that the minister's powers should be at least mellowed by the process of consultation and that this consultation ought to become mandatory rather than discretionary, as the previous amendment set out. They accepted the amendment. There is a new clause in the bill which indicates that the minister shall appoint an advisory council. speechtext: I say that quite sincerely, Mr. Speaker. We want to make sure that somebody from the Atlantic provinces will serve on the council. We want to make sure that there will be on this council somebody who will look after the interests of northern Ontario and other regions.

speechtext:
As a consequence of our amendment being accepted, we feel the bill is now better than it was at the beginning. We ought to examine the record, to see what is the result, at first glance, of any analysis as to the way the program has operated thus far. Sometimes statistics are misleading, yet, on closer examination they usually tell the true story. Let us look at the over-all average of the number of jobs created in the period from, say, September 1 to the end of November, 1970. According to the national average, 42 jobs have been created per approved program.
December 18, 1970

Regional Development Incentives Act
That figure of 42 jobs per approved program does not stand up very well under analysis. If one examines the program closely, one will note that the Atlantic region, with the highest rate of unemployment in the country, had the lowest average number of jobs created per approved application. On the other hand, the province of Ontario, which has enjoyed a traditionally low rate of unemployment, has the highest average for the number of jobs created per approved application. A similar, high average applies to the province of Quebec. This in my view shows a serious weakness in the program. Even if one disregarded the amendment, one could entertain a doubt, to say the least, about whether this program was capable of performing the task that Parliament expected of it, that of creating new jobs.
Let us look at the statistics which apply to other parts of the country. As I said, on a national average 42 jobs have been created per approved application. Let us begin with Newfoundland, which has the highest rate of unemployment in the country and usually has had that unique distinction. For the period September until the end of November, 1970, the number of jobs created per approved application in Newfoundland was three: three jobs were created per approved application. The average figure becomes somewhat higher as one looks at the mainland of Canada. In Prince Edward Island the average number of jobs created per approved job application was 26; in Nova Scotia the average number was 20; in New Brunswick it was 19. Looking at Quebec, one sees that 60 jobs were created per application under this program. In Ontario it increases to 77. It declines as we go further west: in Manitoba it is 14; Saskatchewan, 53; Alberta, 42; British Columbia, 12. British Columbia has a very high rate of unemployment. It has the second highest rate of unemployment in the country.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The number of jobs created per application under this program is the lowest in areas of greatest need, and highest in areas of least need. That does not make sense. This program is not fulfilling its purpose. The purpose of the program was to create jobs in the regionally disadvantaged areas of the country where there is traditionally high unemployment. That is where the program is least effective. We were encouraged by the admission of the deputy minister that the Atlantic Advisory Council has undertaken a study to determine why the program has not been effective in the province of Newfoundland. The new facilities created, as the percentage of the total of applications indicates, show that the Atlantic provinces are well below the national average. Conversely, British Columbia, Quebec and Ontario are above the national average. This indicates that the program has not been effective in creating new jobs in disadvantaged regions. In its present form, the program has had limited effectiveness, especially in the Atlantic provinces.
The amendment before us will do little to correct this serious deficiency. It will provide an added incentive for the Atlantic provinces to offset the incentive provided to Montreal. The amount of the Montreal incentive will be added to that of the Atlantic provinces. The best evidence presented to the committee unequivocally indicated that this would not offset the designation of Montreal; representatives of APEC gave evidence to this effect. Professor Brewis, who was quoted earlier in this debate, gave clear and concise evidence to this effect. Professor Smith the chairman of the Atlantic Advisory Council, was less precise in his evidence before the committee. However, he indicated that before there can be an effective regional development program in this country there must be a strong national economy. If we do not have a strong national economy, the government must forget about regional development, which it is now doing; it must concentrate on uplifting the economy by providing employment in areas of high unemployment in the industrial heartland. This is precisely what the government has done. It now has no regional development policy.
The government has made the regional development program the instrument to combat the cyclical problem in the industrial heartland of Canada. By so doing it has diluted the bill to the point where it is practically useless to areas such as the Atlantic provinces, which is regrettable, Mr. Speaker, because the need is very great. It is anticipated that the rate of unemployment in the Atlantic region this year will exceed 15 per cent. It has already exceeded 10 per cent in Newfoundland, and God knows how high it will go before this winter is over. I point out the statistics to the minister because this is what concerns us about the legislation in its present form. We were not comforted by the evidence of Professor Brewis. This program is all we have and we must try to make the best of it.
We think the government has made a very serious error in judgment by using the regional incentives program as the main weapon to combat the seriously high rate of unemployment in Montreal. We must accept the decision of the government because of our concern about what has happened in Montreal. We have tried to point out the error of the course the government has chosen to follow. We have tried to improve the bill. We hope the bill will alleviate the very serious situation that exists in Montreal.
The minister did not satisfactorily answer the question put to him in committee. Why did he not take advantage of the government organization bill? He could have used the provisions of that bill to deal with the situation. I might add there is a very high rate of unemployment in Vancouver as well. Why not designate Vancouver? The minister could have introduced a "crash" housing program under the National Housing Act to combat unemployment in Montreal. This would have created housing in an area which has a disproportionately high level of substandard housing. It would have achieved two objectives, housing construction which is labour-intensive and it would have provided badly needed jobs and fulfilled a social need. However, the minister did not elect to do this.
