speechtext:
I fail to understand why the government did not use some of the existing programs at its disposal to combat the high unemployment in this country, especially in the cities of Montreal and Vancouver. I hope that when the minister speaks in this debate he will dispel our fears about the way this program has been used and the consequences of the government's action in designating the city of Montreal and part of eastern Ontario. This makes it virtually impossible for provinces such as Newfoundland to compete against Montreal in attracting new job-creating industries, which is the purpose of the program. This concerns us about the program. Members of the New Democratic Party referred to this matter in the debate on their amendment at the report stage of the bill.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Analysis of the program indicates that the highest grants produced the fewest jobs. This, surely, is an anomaly which requires explanation. There must be a reason why this should be so. The hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) referred to this matter and, indeed, the evidence presented to the committee showed that the highest grants did in fact produce the fewest jobs. I hope the minister will explain this situation and dispel our genuine fears on this point.
This is the only development program we have. Until the government brings in a new one we can only hope it will be effective in achieving its objectives. We certainly hope that the study undertaken by the advisory council in Newfoundland will produce a means whereby the program can be effective in that province, a province where this type of assistance is badly needed. Indeed, we hope the program will be effective throughout the Atlantic provinces and that the additional grants will make it possible for us to compete, notwithstanding the designation of Montreal.
We hope this program will work. We have tried to offer constructive criticism and the speeches which will be made by my hon. friends later in this debate will repeat some of our constructive criticism. I want it clearly understood that constructive criticism should not be misconstrued as opposition to the principle of the bill. We
Regional Development Incentives Act support what the minister is trying to do, but we question the way he is doing it. We sincerely hope that the program will be effective, that it will create jobs; but we hope a reasonable explanation can be given of the anomalous situation whereby the highest grants have produced the fewest jobs, and of the disproportion in the number of jobs created in areas of highest unemployment as compared with those in areas of lower unemployment. Having said this, I reiterate the view of the party to which I belong: We support the intent of the legislation but we question the way the government is going about it.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because in my view and in the view of my hon. friends the bill we are discussing is wrong in its policy. It is, as one of the witnesses before the committee said, an administrative monstrosity and it is a negation of the whole idea of regional development properly understood and properly followed.
There is not a thinking person in Canada who does not realize that regional disparity is a problem with top priority in this country. There is not a person in Canada who is not anxious to get rid of the regional disparities. In income, standard of living, employment opportunities, welfare and every other area of our society, the disadvantaged portions of Canada have suffered for decades. We understood that the present government in particular had undertaken to deal with regional disparity in an effective and planned way. The sad and dangerous thing is that this is not the way in which it has been treated. In fact, from the relatively little information the minister has given Parliament, the program appears to be entirely in a shambles.
Every member of this House and every thinking Canadian is concerned about problems in the province of Quebec which were at least in part responsible for the crisis through which we have been passing in the last couple of months. As I said in another debate, I am one Canadian, one Member of Parliament, who is prepared to support any reasonable and effective contribution to raising the economy of Quebec so that unemployment there may be reduced, this winter if possible or in a year or two at least, and so that the basic unhappiness, resentment and frustration may be partly cured in that province. But I say to the minister that this bill and the regional development plan are entirely the wrong vehicle for dealing with the situation in Quebec. One cannot deal with a problem which, one hopes, is temporary, by means of a program which is supposed to have a long-range commitment and objective.
The reasons for the situation in Quebec and in Montreal in particular are quite different from those underlying the situation in the Atlantic provinces or in certain areas of Manitoba. For example, there is no question of transportation costs in Quebec or Montreal, no question that an infrastructure is lacking as there is in the Atlantic provinces. There is no problem about distance from markets, as there is in the Atlantic provinces.
None of the problems which underlie the lack of economic development in the disadvatanged areas is present

December 18, 1970
Regional Development Incentives Act in Montreal or Quebec. What is present in Montreal or Quebec is a consequence of an ill-advised and cruel policy by this government in its so-called fight against inflation. An associated problem in Quebec, as I am sure the minister will want to tell me, is that in recent years certain elements in that province, certain policies, certain groups, have by their nature and behaviour held back the normal amount of private capitalist investment going to Quebec. So there are entirely different grounds for the difficulties they have to face.
These proposals cannot deal with the lack of investment in Quebec as a result of a particular situation there. They cannot deal with the result of the government's dismal monetary, fiscal and investment policies as part of a regional development program intended to improve the disadvantaged areas of the country on a long-term basis. The minister cannot do it, and when he attempts to do it, as he does in this bill, he creates an administrative monstrosity and negates the very objectives which he himself set out when he introduced the original act to which this bill proposes amendments.
I understand that one witness before the committee gave evidence that the program now covers five different kinds of designated areas. There are the designated regions under the original scheme; there are the special areas created within these designated areas. Then we have the prescribed areas where certain other conditions apply. Then we get Montreal, Hull and the three eastern counties of Ontario as areas to which it is intended to apply the particular incentives of the bill before us. In addition there is the new situation in the Atlantic area where they will receive the incentives based on the old program of 25 per cent and $5,000 per job, plus the new program of the additional 10 per cent and an additional $2,000 per job. Mr. Speaker, if this is a sensible, logical program, I am the Emperor of Japan. The minister who is, I am sure, as anxious to deal with these matters as I am, ought to have known better than permit his deputy, who scuttled the anti-poverty program a few years ago, to lead him into the administrative jungle in which he now finds himself.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
There are ways to deal with the special situation of Montreal and Quebec. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has suggested setting up a capital development fund of $150 million, the largest part of which is to go to the province of Quebec. We said at the time that $150 million in terms of the needs of the Canadian economy is both senseless and picayune; that what is required is $750 million or $1 billion if we are to give any real incentive to the improvement of the general economy, and particularly that of the province of Quebec. This would be the proper vehicle for dealing with the situation in Montreal and Quebec, in Cornwall and the three counties of eastern Ontario with which the bill is intended to deal. These areas do not have the problems of the Atlantic area; they must be dealt with in terms of an immediate, planned, large investment program that is not part of the regional development program because these areas are not part of it. You cannot artificially introduce
something that does not belong to the regional development program.
In the Atlantic provinces there is the problem of infrastructure. There are problems of transportation and of private corporations that do not see a profit in the Atlantic economy. The policies that the minister and his department have followed show no element of planning, of direction, and constitute ad hoc planning of the worst possible kind. The minister jumps from one thing to another without reference to area. One of the witnesses from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, I think Mr. Flemming whose evidence I quickly read today, told the committee that what they have had in the Atlantic provinces is merely an increase in existing industry. He said that almost nothing new had been introduced. I will take his word for that since my observations during my visits there have shown me the same thing. From what I know about the grants that have been made to small businesses, there has not been any planning for industrial or economic development, as Mr. Flemming on behalf of APEC told the committee. It is simply a case of giving money to any business that looks O.K.
We also have a terrific time lag here. This should be kept in mind when we talk of Montreal, Quebec and Cornwall. According to the information the members of the House had toward the end of October, there were an estimated 18,362 jobs that it was intended to create with a commitment of $102,579,442. However, as of this week only $3.4 million had actually been paid out. I do not blame the department for this, though I suspect that part of the reason for it has been a great deal of bureaucratic movement in reverse, a sort of two steps backwards, one step forward process which frequently happens in this sort of case. But even if that is not the case, what this situation does underline is the immense time lag between the commitment of some expenditure on businesses that have come into the plan and the actual paying out of the money.
According to Mr. Flemming-I did not read in the evidence a denial on behalf of the minister or his deputy-it takes 16 weeks from the time of the making of an application to receiving an offer from the department. Then there is a further time lapse in order to build a plant if a new plant is required, to get machinery if new machinery is required, to import equipment if new equipment is required or to set up a new work force if a new work force is required. These things cannot be done overnight; they take months, sometimes years. As I have said, to attempt to deal with the situation in Montreal and Cornwall by the regional development route is to heap illogic upon illogic.
Having tried to study and understand the whole policy, my major objection to it is that there is no plan regarding regional development. I have seen no evidence that the department and its advisers have sat down and asked themselves what the Atlantic region needs over the next 15 years to raise its economy to a level that approximates the national average. I am not talking about merely expanding some little industry already in the Atlantic provinces; we may be required to introduce completely

December 18, 1970

new industry and new concepts into the area. This is the way the problem is tackled in other countries and it is done in this way because there is not the same stupid, reactionary, doctrinaire commitment to deal only with private enterprise and private corporations.
It is true that there is no country in the world, at least no country I know of, that does not have a problem in regard to regional disparity. To take the Communist countries first, Russia has such a problem, as do China, Poland and Yugoslavia. The same is true in Italy and France, and to a lesser extent in West Germany and Britain. Even in the Scandinavian countries, where populations are small, there are disadvantaged areas vis-a-vis the national average in those countries. In other words, this is a world problem, not one that Canada alone faces.
I admit that this problem is not soluble overnight, in a year or even in five years. But we have to make a start on solving the problem. The way in which other countries have started to solve it is not by waving carrots in front of the noses of private enterprisers and echoing the stupidities which private enterprisers have echoed for decades. We must solve this problem by doing what has been done in Italy, France, West Germany, Britain and other democratic countries, namely, by having a plan for the location of industry, a plan that is related to the indigenous resources and skills of the area, a plan that takes account of the total economy and the regional economy and relates the one to the other. Such a plan has a life for a period of years, instead of jumping from one alleged crisis to another.
It is this utter lack of planning in the minister's department that has, in my opinion, made his department a shambles. This is why this legislation is bound to fail, though I know the minister will not agree and neither, perhaps, will the official opposition agree. On any proposal for planning and public investment, my party remains alone. I am not unhappy about that. I would rather stand alone with the conviction that I am right than merely follow the herd, and I do not apologize for that. As I say, the action the government is now taking is bound to fail.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Ever since 1963 we have been promised a Canada Development Corporation. Unless I am mistaken, every Throne Speech since a Liberal government has been in power, whether under right hon. Mr. Pearson or under its present leader, has promised a Canada Development Corporation. We still do not have it. The way to deal with the Montreal and Cornwall situations, and the way to deal with many aspects of the disadvantages the Atlantic region suffers, is to have a Canada Development Corporation simultaneously with a regional development plan, so you would have a pool of investment under the control of the government which could be used to raise the economies of all parts of Canada in a planned and sensible way. That is what we should have.
Because we do not have a Canada Development Corporation and because the minister does not have a pool of investment to which he can turn, except the funds the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury
Regional Development Incentives Act Board (Mr. Drury) make available from time to time, he does this kind of senseless thing. I say to him that this bill is senseless. Hon. Members who spoke earlier today were right when they said this bill completely negates the regional development plan. The people of the Atlantic provinces are right to fear that as the result of this proposal they will get even less than they have received until now. The people of Quebec are right in feeling that their problems are being dealt with in a useless, flippant and almost silly way, and that they cannot look forward to a real solution to the problems they have faced and which Canada has had to face.
Of course I know that this bill will pass because the government has decided on it. However, I say, first, that it is a bad bill in itself and, second, that it destroys the concept of regional expansion. Third, it is another example of complete lack of economic and social planning. Finally, it will be of no use whatsoever in solving the unemployment situation in Montreal this winter, and probably of little use even a year or two years from now.
When we look at what the minister has accomplished a year or two from now, we will find that this minister, who has a big heart and a desire to do this job well, will be a failure because of the way he is proceeding and because the work is unplanned. He will be a failure because of the mixed-up monstrosity he has created with this bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that we are debating such a vitally important subject under the pressure of a Christmas recess deadline. There is nothing more important in the country at this time than the necessity of dealing with a problem which has been with Canada since confederation-the problem of regional economic disparity. This was one of the major topics discussed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during the 1968 election campaign. It is one of the recurring issues which crop up at federal-provincial conferences on constitutional matters and also in respect of other areas of government. Because the government is taking this precipitous action to deal with a fundamental problem on a crisis basis, we find ourselves involved in a debate that can only aggravate the tensions which exist in Canada as a result of regional economic disparity.
Other members who have spoken during the debate have pointed out the government's failure to deal with this problem on a long-term basis. This has been the peculiar approach of the present government to economic matters. Just two or three weeks ago we had a budget brought down on the basis of a crisis precipitated by the troubles the province of Quebec has experienced in the past few weeks. That budget has since been described by various authorities on taxation matters as a non-budget.
To indicate that I am not prejudiced about this matter, I should like to quote a new Liberal voice from western Canada. I refer to the new Liberal provincial leader in Manitoba, Mr. Asper, who became well known for his understanding of tax problems as a result of his widely read book "The Benson Iceberg". His response to the

December 18, 1970
Regional Development Incentives Act non-budget was in the following terms, and I quote from the Brandon Sun of December 4, 1970:
"It's a budget designed to bolster the eastern economy while it should have created job opportunities on the Prairies so eastern unemployment could have drifted here", Mr. Asper said in an interview.
I should like to speak during the few minutes at my disposal this afternoon about the western approach to government initiative in the area of regional economic development and the whole program of diversification and dispersal of industry in order to bring about a more rational distribution of population, financial resources and political power. These problems have been discussed in Parliament since the end of World War II with increasing intensity. As a result, the government has moved gradually and cautiously into this area of responsibility.
I remember that one of the first private members' resolutions sponsored related to the necessity of government action to ensure diversification and dispersal of industry throughout the nation. There was considerable progress made in the latter part of the 1950s and the early part of the 1960s when special plans and programs were designed to deal with problems facing the Mari-times. We have heard several spokesmen from the Mari-times who have presented their case in typically eloquent terms. The program for northern development also came to the fore. There were also the special programs to deal with the peculiar problems of western Canada and the designated area program designed to deal with pockets of unemployment in urban centres. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was designed to offset the rural-urban drift which was reaching chronic proportions.
Unfortunately, during the latter part of the 1960s the government's policies both in respect of urban growth and the agricultural industry have tended to aggravate rather than solve this problem of population drift from rural communities to urban centres. This has resulted in a crisis atmosphere which is becoming all too obvious in our huge metropolis areas. Unfortunately, also, the legislation before us today is designed to deal with one of these crisis areas on an ad hoc basis. As has already been stated by spokesmen on this side of the House this approach will destroy the fundamental purpose of the DREE program.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
If the process of continuing planning which has been gradually established over the past 15 years is interrupted by the use of legislation to deal with an immediate crisis situation, the program unfortunately will become so badly distorted that it will, as I have already indicated, aggravate regional disparity and create a growing tension and dissension in the whole area of national unity, rather than relieve the problem. 1 have already quoted one western Liberal authority in this regard. Perhaps the most apt description of what is taking place in respect of the government's initiative is that the program of regional disparity is being changed to one of political disparity which in the old days was known as pork-barrel politics.
Again, as an indication that this is not the prejudiced pronouncement of a member of the opposition, I should like to go back to the Liberal authority to whom I have already referred. I quote from the Brandon Sun of November 26 this year as follows:
The leader of the provincial Liberal Party told the Brandon Liberal Women's Association that Manitoba, in fact the entire Prairie region, is a victim of an "anarchistic and outdated" governmental structure-
Further on the article reads:
In a hard-hitting 70-mlnute address, Mr. Asper said he intends to travel throughout Canada "to tell how confederation has denied us equality of economic opportunity and reduced us to the status of second-class citizens."
Then he deals directly with the problem which we are discussing this afternoon.
About 33 per cent of Manitoba's one million people live below the poverty line.
"This 33 per cent figure speaks a great deal," Mr. Asper said. "It is higher than the 27 per cent figure for Quebec and everyone bleeds for Quebec. I also bleed for Quebec but I bleed more for Manitoba."
I agree wholeheartedly with the sentiment expressed by the leader of the Manitoba Liberal party. Coming closer to home, we have another Liberal spokesman from the west, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson), who comes back to the theme repeatedly. He has expressed continuing concern and I hope similar sentiments will be expressed during the course of this debate. A year before Mr. Asper expressed this concern, the minister is quoted in the Winnipeg Tribune of November 17, 1969, as follows:
In a strong speech to delegates attending the annual meeting of the Manitoba Liberal Party Sunday, Mr. Richardson warned that growth of eastern Canada at the expense of the western region must be brought to an end.
Further on we find these words:
He made it abundantly clear western Canada will not stand by idly while government controls are centralized further in Ottawa and economic powers are allowed to concentrate in Toronto and Montreal.
This is the old formula of dividing and conquering, because strong words like that from spokesmen of the Liberal Party in Western Canada of course receive the plaudits of the public. Words of that kind also have a very divisive effect upon the Canadian body politic. Parliament is the place those sentiments should be expressed. I trust that some western Liberal spokesmen who sit in this House of Commons and represent western constituencies will seize the opportunity provided by this debate to express those sentiments when they will have the most effect, while the minister is in the House listening to the voice of western Canada as expressed by Members of Parliament. Unfortunately, the minister cannot hear such expressions out on the hustings where their whole intent is to divide and conquer.
Worse than the failure to plan on a continuous basis to deal with the fundamental problem of regional disparity, we find that some of the recent program initiatives of the government have been working at cross-purposes. I should like to refer to one or two obvious examples of

December 18, 1970

this. The problem of transportation in western Canada is always with us. We have the continuous downgrading of railway transportation in the west. What is more to the point, in this day and age when air transporation is becoming increasingly important we find the government is allowing its regional air policies to be downgraded by gradual erosion through decisions made by the Canadian Transport Commission.
Back in the middle fifties in the province of Manitoba we had adequate class A air service from Winnipeg right through to Calgary. Air Canada provided that service initially. Then Air Canada relinquished the responsibility to a regional air carrier, TransAir, along with a subsidy. In the past two years that subsidy has been removed. In a day when air transportation is of the utmost importance if we are to have any hope of encouraging industrial development, we find that the regional service at the western lateral between Winnipeg, Brandon, Yorkton, Regina and Calgary has been completely discontinued.
Last year, for example, the city of Brandon lost its class A service through to Winnipeg and Regina. This was done quite surreptitiously. In the last few weeks TransAir has even discontinued its daily service between Winnipeg and Regina. We are moving back to the horse-and-buggy days, instead of moving forward in the space age or air age when if we are to have any hope of benefiting from the government's regional development program we must ensure to prospective industry that there is adequate, first-class air service.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
This is happening in face of the expenditure of millions of dollars for new airfields both in the Toronto and the Montreal regions. I can understand why Liberal spokesmen in the west are criticizing so vehemently the Liberal administration in Ottawa for their neglect in this respect. I only wish they would use the forum provided by Parliament, instead of shouting from the rooftops, on the hustings and then remaining deathly still and quiet here in the high court of public opinion.
I could also mention, of course, the confusion that was caused by the downgrading of the postal service within the past year when several communities disappeared completely in various parts of western Canada because of the arbitrary closure of rural post offices. Fortunately, we have a man in charge of that department now who understands the essence of regional development and the basis of rural problems and he has reversed that decision; but untold damage was done because of the government's failure to appreciate the real issues of regional development in western Canada.
As a result of this policy, or lack of policy, and of the planning, or lack of planning, on the part of the government we have this continued concentration in huge urban metropolises which creates problems of pollution beyond man's capacity to cope with, where the rate of crime soars, where urban guerrilla activities become a matter of serious concern and where, as is happening in some of the large centres in the United States, the problems of urban organization become almost unmanageable. This
Regional Development Incentives Act government's answer is to add insult to injury and to indroduce ad hoc programs that will only aggravate rather than resolve and assist in remedying some of these problems.
In conclusion I would like to give a specific example of the government's failure to give equal emphasis to economic problems and crises in various parts of Canada. I refer to its failure to deal with the phasing-out of military bases in western Canada in a manner designed to have the least possible economic impact on the communities concerned. In the province of Manitoba we have lost two military bases within the past several months. Two thousand seven hundred jobs were represented by those two air bases. This is more than twice the number of job opportunities created under the program of the depart-merit in the last year.
So we are going backward rather than forward. It does not have to be so, because there has been ample warning that in the government's reassessment of the military requirements for Canada there has been four or five years warning. The base at Portage has been kept open even though there is a housing shortage that will require the expenditure of substantial sums of money in order to supply adequate housing for the increased personnel there. During the recent crisis in Quebec when military personnel had to be flown from Shilo to Montreal on an emergency basis, the Rivers airport, which is one of the best airports in Canada, had to be reopened temporarily because the Portage base was not adequate to meet this requirement. Millions of dollars have been spent at the Rivers air base in the last few years to repair the runways because it was felt that it would be one of the basic air force training units in Canada for a long time to come.
However, suddenly it is phased out of existence, and since the announcement was made in September there has been no concrete indication by the government that there are alternative programs to use the excellent facilities at this base. Representations have been made by the local communities involved who have come to Ottawa at their own expense on several occasions. Representatives of the provincial government of Manitoba have made pilgrimages to Ottawa. We have the promise that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) himself will be coming to Manitoba early in the new year when he will announce plans and policies to deal with the economic crisis that has been created by this situation.
I hope that in the interests of an adequate, fair and non-discriminatory approach to problems of regional disparity the minister will be as generous to western Canada as he is to the areas that are being specially designated under the legislation before us. If Ottawa does not operate on a fair basis, the protests that I have read briefly this afternoon by the Liberal minister from Manitoba, the speeches that he makes regularly on the hustings rather than in the House of Commons, will rise to an unhappy chorus that can only have a serious impact on national unity in Canada. Then there are the statements of the new Liberal leader, Mr. Asper, which I quoted earlier. People will begin to take him seriously if

December 18, 1970
Regional Development Incentives Act
he goes on this crusade, as he says he will, across Canada, and again we will have increasing problems of national unity which are created by economic difficulties rather than cultural or symbolic matters.
As previous speakers have said, there is nothing much we the opposition can do about this legislation. The government is prepared to push it through regardless of any protests. It has been brought in during the dying hours of this part of the session of Parliament. The government has its disciplined majority. In the interests of a united Canada from sea to sea, I urge the government and the minister, as he contemplates the problems in western Canada, to act with the generosity and expedition that he is employing in the matter under discussion today.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on the legislation before us for third reading, I assure the House that it is my intention to speak very briefly and to deal with only one or two points in connection with the over-all incentives program. Just over a year ago we passed the Regional Development Incentives Act. This act was to provide incentives for the development of productive employment opportunities in designated regions which require special measures to facilitate economic expansion and social adjustment. Bill C-205 which we are discussing seeks to amend that legislation. There are several areas where I feel other changes should be made and I welcome this opportunity to once again draw them to the attention of the minister and the House.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The specific objectives of the Regional Development Incentives Act were to foster industrial development in slow-growth areas. A number of these designated areas have been set up throughout Canada. My constituency of Kootenay West is located in one of them. To date, however, relatively few new jobs have been created as a result of this designation. There is an indication, however, that the several industrial committees which have been set up to promote and encourage the establishment of industries within their respective districts will obtain results. There is no doubt that it takes a long tline ^ to contact interested industrial groups and have them visit the area to assess the possibilities. [Mr. Dlnsdale.l

It would be a tragedy to encourage the development of certain types of industry in a prime tourist area. Such development could only ruin the potential for tourism. That is why I would urge the minister to apply financial incentives to the development of the tourist industry. That is why I am requesting the government to add it to the over-all picture and make the program apply from the east to the west of Canada.
In speaking about the tourist industry I would point out to the government that this is something we can sell time and time again. It is not depleted as is mining or logging. Once developed, it is there for all time and can be sold to people who like to visit these areas. As long as we do not destroy our environment through foolish development, it will endure. If we want to stop unwise economic development in some areas we must clearly indicate now that tourism is the key industry to be covered. Then we can start long-range planning for any area suited to it.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not spend any more time on this bill because I know other speakers want to deal with points which have not been raised. In closing I would say I am alarmed at the hodgepodge that has taken place in our regional development planning. It is just patch upon patch. The government does not seem to have a clear idea of its direction. As several speakers have already pointed out, there are five different types of designated area in Canada. This cannot lead to adequate or proper planning. I agree it would have been better for the nation to have had a Canada development plan under an act, with adequate funds for development purposes. Then perhaps we could have proceeded along these lines in an orderly manner. I urge the minister to seriously consider the tremendous impact which the inclusion of tourism incentives in the Regional Development Incentives Act would have on all parts of Canada. [DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Our latest difficulty arises from the freight rate increase, and reference was made to that during the question period. There has been no other opportunity for members from Atlantic Canada to refer to it. I wish to quote from an article by Lyndon Watkins in today's Globe and Mail:
Maritime potato producers are digging in for a determined battle with the railways over freight rate increases and sharply increased auxiliary charges which they say will add 70 per cent to transportation costs on export shipments through St. John
and Halifax.
What is being done about this by the involved planning of the minister's department? An injustice is being inflicted upon the potato producers of two provinces of Atlantic Canada, the chief contributors toward agricultural income. It will be a serious blow to many people,
not only those actively involved in agriculture, but those other citizens depending upon the success of those people. There should be a frontal attack by all departments of government on those aspects of national policy which make one region or another uniquely at a disadvantage because of these national policies. With all the powers that the minister has, even if he were as good as some people might think, he and his department could not cope with these problems. The whole government must be seized of them.
I do not enjoy being looked upon as a special pleader. We in the Maritimes grow a little weary about having to bring forward eternally for national consideration the problems with which we have to cope. However, for over a century we have had disadvantages against which we have had to struggle. Many of these have come as a result of uniting with the rest of the country. I think it can be said, without special pleading and without chauvinism, that we have never had our fair share of the fruits of federation. A very clear example can be seen by looking at the map of Canada in 1867. There was a union of four provinces at that time. They were not large provinces. A generation or so later two of the provinces had grown into vast structures. They extended northward and in one case westward. They became geographical giants and giants in other ways.
Other provinces were added. They were at first small and they grew. The province of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) was once the postage stamp province. The territories around these provinces were developed by united and confederated Canada. As the years went by, not one acre was added to the area of the two oldest provinces, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. This also applies to Prince Edward Island. As new frontiers were opened, the three provinces by the sea were shut out of that particular kind of expansion. Therefore, we do not hesitate to say that we have rights.
We have reason to suggest to the federal government that the inequities which national policies have inflicted upon our region should be corrected by the only agency capable of doing this, the federal government. What we have before us is at best a palliative, at worst a weakening of the existing structure. Perhaps it is a well inten-tioned effort to improve the situation in the province of Quebec which, in economic terms, has apparently become far worse than many hon. members from that area expected. Mr. Speaker, I participate in this debate with mixed feelings. I realize that this part of the session is limping to a close. There is a sort of curfew on how long members can participate in the debate on Bill C-205. This is one of the more important pieces of legislation to be dealt with by this Parliament. I do not say that because I represent an Atlantic area constituency, but because I am a federal legislator in the House of Commons. I recognize the fact that there is a curtailment of time and that members opposite, especially in the ministry, deserve a break. I think all members deserve a break, not because of what we have produced in this House, but because of the stress and strain that members of the cabinet had to sustain and suffer this fall. Hopefully, with this Christmas recess, we will be able to regenerate and return to do constructive work and perhaps avoid the type of bill that we are debating today.
One of my misgivings about this bill is its title, "An Act to amend the Regional Development Incentives Act". Some of what I say will obviously be repetitive. Some members opposite may think it is all repetitive. However,
I wish to add a couple of thoughts to the pot, not in the hope that there will be a great conversion of the minister on the road to Damascus or that there will be any change in the substance of the bill, but when the next session of this Parliament commences and the problems still exist throughout Canada on a regional basis perhaps we will appreciate the folly of our ways in approving Bill C-205.
I protest Bill C-205, not because of a parochial or provincial interest, but because the very title of the bill is a misnomer. While this is a bill to amend the The Regional Development Incentives Act, as a result of the regulations the minister is going to pronounce following the passage of this bill, it will no longer be a regional act. It will, in fact, be a national development incentives act. Every member of the House should be aware of what is taking place, what is going on. I must say I listened with a great deal of respect to the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and to the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), who led the Conservative group in the deliberations before the committee and who contributed in a most constructive way this afternoon. My hon. friend from Hillsborough talked more in a historical perspective.

I shall not belabour the obvious problems of the Atlantic area or the problems of the Gaspe area or the problems of certain parts of the Prairies. Before these amendments came before Your Honour, these were the regions of economic disparity which could look to a federal gov-
Regional Development Incentives Act ernment for unique assistance in a most enlightened way. I shall not belabour the past in that way but I have been somewhat surprised by the vacuum of silence on the part of members from other parts of Canada who have made no contribution either plus or minus on Bill C-205. If I were a government member from Ontario, and there are a good many of them, I would be more concerned about the implications of this bill than I am as a member from the Atlantic area.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that except for some members on the opposite side who were on the committee dealing with regional economic expansion, not too many appreciate what is being done by this bill. Industry in, say, Ontario, will now be competing with industry across the boundary in Quebec. On one side of the boundary there will be a 25 per cent incentive, which was the amount under the old act, because of regional disparity, but as a result of this amendment there will be either a 25 per cent or a 10 per cent incentive depending on whether the industry is in Montreal or St. Jean or nearer the Ontario border. The effect of this three-tier incentive program which the minister has proposed to stimulate activity in some areas which have experienced unfortunate difficulties in the last few months and in the last few years, combined with the 25 per cent grant which presently exists under the old bill and the 10 per cent which the Atlantic area is to get making a 35 per cent set-up, will be to create potentially serious problems for any organized industrial expansion in any part of the country.
The only explanation which comes to my mind for the lack of contributions from members from all parts of the country, not just from an area of economic disparity be it the Atlantic area or not, is the restriction on time. For the purpose of the record, because this has been referred to in a general way, I want to outline the unconscionable haste with which this bill has moved from first reading on December 4, which as Your Honour knows is just a formality, see to the second reading debate on December 10. Then, for the first time, between 3.40 p.m. and 5 o'clock, it was debated for an hour and twenty minutes and between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. for two hours. On Friday, December 11, this bill was debated for another hour and twenty minutes in the morning and another two hours in the afternoon. On Monday, December 14, it was finally referred to a committee after being debated for a grand total of one hour. In total, up to today, seven hours and forty minutes have been spent on a bill which I suggest to all members of this House affects all regions of this country.
While the catalyst, with the utmost sincerity of the minister and his advisers, was special problems and unique situations in Quebec and Montreal, the full ramifications of this bill affect this nation from coast to coast. I suggest what I have outlined is a sad commentary on the House of Commons. Many people outside this august chamber wonder how relevant we are, and how realistic our debates are, when a bill which is fundamental to the industrial and economic fabric of this land has been considered for only seven hours and forty

December 18, 1970
Regional Development Incentives Act minutes in this House. Of course, we all know it was discussed in committee, and it did receive three or four days of rather strenuous sessions of committee debate. But committee debate does not as yet, with the facilities that we have to propagate propaganda or policies, call it what you will, generate public interest. It might be just coincidence.
The minister states there is necessity for almost a brevity of debate because these proposals are supposed to be implemented on January 1. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, if the situation is as fundamental and serious as the minister told us in committee, then it is certainly a sad reflection on the planning of his department that this bill comes to this House in the dying days of this part of the session after receiving a grand total of seven hours and forty minutes of House debate. How does the country even appreciate it, as other members have said? How can people begin to study the implications? Certainly, until we got into committee I suggest that at least half the members of the Regional Economic Expansion committee did not really fully appreciate what was going on.
I want to deal, Mr. Speaker, with this bill in a relatively short period of time, but I shall not apoligize for taking my full time for the reasons I have just stated. I shall express my views on the basis of the principle of the bill as I see it, and the problems of the bill and I shall be covering many of the areas that have been very well documented by other members so I shall be brief. And I shall make a prophecy about this bill which, I suggest, whether it is right or wrong, should be at least stated so that we do not live in the unreal world in which we so often find ourselves in the House of Commons because we are afraid to say what we all talk about behind the curtains. We are not supposed to say these things on the floor of the House because they might offend sensibilities or be misinterpreted. As far as I am concerned, I am getting so fed up about the danger of being misinterpreted that I think arteriosclerosis is inhibiting the positive, frank point of view often expressed by all members of the House. And I am as much at fault in that respect as anybody.
But coming to the principle of the bill, there is no doubt, and I want to make this most clear, we all support the objective and hope it is achieved. The minister, perhaps in the emotion and excitement of second reading when he was a little impatient, made some most unfortunate suggestions about my hon. friend from Hillsborough who has contributed, as far as I am concerned, in a most positive way to a true one Canada regardless of how we all define it. This was most unfortunate. However, as I said in the beginning, I understand and sympathize with the minister, especially since he has been under abnormal stress and strain. Let us hope we get out of this place so that the minister, who is a pretty fine fellow although politically I am pretty apprehensive of him, will not, perhaps, say things that he will regret. speechtext:
In any event, it has nothing to do with the merits of the bill. Since the hon. member for Calgary South wants to entertain some idiocies, let me transgress for a moment and get just a little bit political. Let me point out the paradox in which this chamber now finds itself. The government ran an election campaign on two mains planks, one of which was elimination of regional economic disparity. In this bill the government are eliminating regional economic disparity and substituting national economic development. National economic development may be fine and we are all for it, but they must remember that there are precise and chronic problems in regions that do not enjoy the full economic growth that some areas enjoy.
In the last election campaign, the government ran under the banner of one Canada and the elimination of regional economic disparity. The hon. member for Calgary South-and when he runs again in the next election campaign we will see whether he will still have his seat in this House-is supporting a government that no longer preaches the platitude of one Canada but is now dividing Canada, in effect, into have and have-not areas.
By expanding the designated areas, the bill is now including half of Canada within such areas, the other half remaining outside. This is a pretty ironic commentary on the political life of this country. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) claimed during the last election campaign that he had the answer to the provincial and perennial question of the two solitudes. The two solitudes of the past have now become the economic solitudes of the present.
In addition to converting regional economic policy with long-term goals into cyclical unemployment policies of
[Mr. Nowlan.)
December 18, 1970

short-term duration, the bill is placing the future growth and industrial fabric of the land in the hands of one man, namely the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. No matter how wise, rational or benevolent is the minister, he has all the frailties and failings of a human being. I suggest this is the important difference between the original regional incentives bill and Bill C-205 that is now amending the act.
Under the government reorganization bill that created the minister's department, the minister was given discretion over which applications to allow and how much money to grant those applicants. However, under the regulations passed pursuant to the bill the authority and discretion of the minister was restricted to areas of economic disparity. I suggest that the timeless problems in these well demarcated areas of economic disparity helped to dilute and to define the unlimited discretion of the minister. As the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) and other members have said, these pockets of disparity can be pinpointed on the map. This bill is now extending the boundaries of the designated areas to include part of the industrial heartland of Canada. In effect, the minister is being given unlimited discretion effectively to direct the placement of new industry in more than half of Canada, and to define what is to be the expansion of existing industry.
I suggest that the effect of any decision that the minister might make will last for a longer time than any restriction that is imposed upon him in the bill. His signature to any application for assistance will survive any member of this House. As a parliamentarian this is the basic issue here, the arbitrary, unfettered and unrestricted discretion that is now being given to the minister, albeit for the most laudable objectives.
Reference was made earlier to Mr. Howe, who was also a noted economic expansionist and industrialist, a man who obviously did a lot to develop the economy of Canada. It was not too many years ago that he asked "What's a million?". I suggest that Mr. Howe was being prophetic, because "what's a million?" is pretty irrelevant in terms of the millions that this minister will have at his disposal and direction in order to help stimulate and expand industry in new areas of the country including, as I say, a large part of the industrial heartland of Canada. This issue here is whether any minister who has been elected to legislate should be able to dictate so effectively the future course of the economic development of this country. This is my objection to this bill.
Another issue which has been hit upon by hon. members who have spoken is the question whether a regional development program should be a policy for curing cyclical unemployment; whether long range plans should be merged into short run priorities, or whether the permanent solution of problems in areas of regional economic disparity should be diluted, perhaps even destroyed, by bypassing problems of admittedly critical importance but hopefully only of a temporary nature; whether in this bill the chronically ill parts of the country will not become even sicker, notwithstanding that there is a crisis in Canada in areas that have been geographically
Regional Development Incentives Act defined. I do not want to misquote the minister, but he said he wanted a 15-year program. He said he did not want measures of expediency, yet we have them in this bill. I suggest he will have to exercise the wisdom of Solomon in the administration of his proposed cure in order to prevent the spawning of increased stresses and strains to the fabric of this nation.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Basically, what is proposed is the concept of arbitrary discretion to deal with long-term regional development programs and long-term social and employment objectives. I do not want to repeat what has been said about the specific problems, and I am sure that will make many hon. members happy. I would like to believe that this bill is senseless, because if it is my fears would not be justified. I think there is something hidden in it.
Undoubtedly there will be administrative problems. When Professor Brewis testified before the committee he outlined the types of selective assistance available at different levels, 10 per cent, 25 per cent and 35 per cent, depending on the area. I suggest the problems we have in respect of regional development and national economic development will be compounded by this bill. If anything this bill takes on the aspect of a Trojan horse. It may be that many people in the country will look at this measure as the Trojan horse was looked upon. We all recall that the Trojan horse was inhabited by soldiers and when these people realize the enemies inherrent in this bill they will then know its potential for inhibiting production. In many aspects, this bill is just as deceptive as the Trojan horse.
Professor Brewis also suggested this measure would not create jobs, as the minister suggests. He refers to the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the $130 million to be used in this regard. He also mentioned the cost of $5,000 per job under the DREE program. This man is a professor who has written many books on regional economic disparity. He suggests that if you use the $130 million at an estimated rate of $5,000 per job, these incentives will create a potential of between 25,000 and 30,000 jobs. We all know that we have between
600,000	and 700,000 unemployed at the present time.
I should like to know where special incentives should be made available. If we believe the minister, this provision in the bill is supposed to stimulate growth. Where is this growth to be stimulated. Does it provide incentives to attract existing industry interested in locating in Canada. This is a factor which bothers me, having regard to the Atlantic provinces. It would also bother me if I lived in Ontario.
These incentives must be held out to attract industry to newly designated areas. The amount in relation to Montreal and other areas is 10 per cent. That might be sufficient to attract some industries to locate in those areas rather than in other parts of the country. We must keep in mind the differential involved, because 10 per cent in respect of a large industry likely to locate in the Montreal area is much different from 35 per cent in respect of a small industry locating in another designated area.

December 18, 1970
Regional Development Incentives Act
On December 8 the Prime Minister made a speech in Saint John, New Brunswick. On page 5 of his press release he refers to the potential markets in New England for manufactured goods from the Atlantic Provinces. Let me quote from this press release as follows:
Industry is now coming to New Brunswick and to the Atlantic provinces. It is attracted in part by the availability of resources, of transportation, of a skilled labour force, and in part by the government incentives such as those offered by the federal department of Regional Economic Expansion.
It then reads:
As it comes, those factors that I have mentioned should be taken into account to ensure a long-range, healthy type of development.
As I mentioned earlier, the special incentives set up in Bill C-205 may very well have a counter effect to that which the Prime Minister had in mind three or four days before this bill was placed before this House for second reading. It might be that in St. Jean, Quebec, you would have greater access to the New England market for manufactured goods than you would have in Saint John, New Brunswick, because this 10 per cent incentive for designated areas is very deceptive.
We heard evidence before the committee that during the existence of this measure some 400 applications had been made, but that only six applicants had received the maximum grant. I understand three of those were in New Brunswick, one in Prince Edward Island, one in Quebec and one in Saskatchewan. There was an indication in the press release that the Atlantic area was to receive the same 10 per cent incentive as the designated area around Montreal. In this regard, there will also be a ministerial discretion. When you consider these things, together with the fact that a maximum grant has only been given to six applicants during the history of this measure, it does not require a complicated computer to realize that the 10 per cent incentive in a heavily populated area will have a much greater effect than a 35 per cent grant to a small company in the Atlantic area.
When the minister appeared before the committee, he indicated he wanted to balance that which was being granted new areas with what had previously been offered in the Atlantic areas. I do not read in any ulterior motives, but the fact is that only six applicants have received the full grant. It is deceptive and highly illusionary to suggest that the 10 per cent to newly designated areas will be offset by the same 10 per cent in the Atlantic area.
It should be obvious that industry of greater magnitude will establish in Montreal and other heavily populated areas in the industrial heartland of this country. A maximum grant of 35 per cent for a smaller plant in a smaller populated area will not be equivalent to a 10 per cent grant to a bigger industry in these populated areas. A great deal will depend on how the minister exercises his discretion. If he is not careful, he could effectively stifle new industry in the Atlantic area and smother existing industry. In this way this measure would run completely counter to the direction the Prime Minister
mentioned four days after this bill was given first reading and just before it was presented to the House for second reading. I wonder whether these two ministers ever got together in this regard. The Prime Minister may have been sincere in the speech he made in Saint John, but what he suggested was almost as deceptive as some parts of this bill.
There are other specific problems I could mention, but the government has decided in its wisdom to take this course in helping those areas which need special help. They will have to live with it.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Then, we have my prophecy in respect of this bill. This is my third, perhaps my shortest but more serious point. I still believe, no matter whether the minister be a Conservative, a Liberal, an NDP or of what political stripe, he should not have the unfettered discretion this bill would give him, although for the most laudable objective. Fortunately, the minister did acquiesce in the committee and agree that there shall be a council to sort of supervise the administration of the act. We will be most interested to see what form that council takes, because we know it will not have a legislative effect but only an effect after the fact. However, I would not wish to be in the minister's shoes with the discretion he will have. It is a fantastic commentary on the evolution of politics, at a time when governments delegate authority to delegate authority, that there has not been an expression on this question of the delegation of the appropriate power. I am sure the minister will try to exercise this power most sincerely. But if I were a political animal in any part of the country, which I am, I would be exposed to and involved in almost unnatural pressures to put my signature to an application in my area, or if I were from British Columbia to an application for that area, in respect of the particular problems which arise.
I am amazed that there has not been more of a complaint, because the new designated areas remove part of the restriction we had before. The minister, and any minister, obviously had to look at the facts of life before he granted or disapproved a loan. The history of the economy of a particular area would, in large measure, indicate whether or not a prospective industry would be a viable industry. But when a minister begins exercising discretionary power in half of this country, and particularly in the industrial heartland, it is an entirely different matter.
The other point of principle was the question of the mixture of long-term development or regional policies now being instituted, diluted and/or destroyed by shortterm cyclical policies. But the principle of this bill again contains a sort of an irony. Again this should involve and interest all members of this House. A government which campaigned and won a strong mandate on the one-Canada theme not too long ago, and which at federal-provincial conferences has been completely against any form of special status anywhere, has by this bill, again for laudable objectives, sought to give special status to one-half of Canada. I suggest it is thereby making two Canadas.

December 18, 1970

Although it is passing strange-and perhaps if it were not so serious I could be more humorous about it-I suggest we will be faced with Bill C-205, amendments to Bill C-205 and amendments to other bills to help particular parts of this country. While it might be Quebec and Montreal today, it could be another part of the country tomorrow, unless this ministry starts to get tuned into the times and develops some viable constitutional policies which reflect the realities of this land. This is just a patch work job at best. How soon will it be before the Canadian people start to ask us if we are to provide particular funds to help particular parts of the country for various constitutional purposes. That is part of the gut issue in a bill that is anonymously called, an act to amend the Regional Development Incentives Act. We know we cannot continue in this unreal world much longer. We are not all the same. I am glad the minister is sponsoring this bill because if we can have the economic two Canadas which this bill would establish, then surely the minister would have some flexibility in respect of his dealings with his great friend and colleague the Prime Minister of this land.
Perhaps the minister could persuade the Prime Minister to adopt some flexibility in his constitutional stance, so that instead of having repeated constitutional discussions that accomplish nothing we could start to have the give and take of ideas that would reflect the realities of the land and our regional differences. I am not speaking about French or English and/or third force, but that is part of it. I say we are living in a dreamland if we believe this country is all the same. Quebec is different, and thank God it is different in so many ways. But let us not have this smokescreen that has polluted constitutional discussions, because unless we start to wake up and face reality we will have more bills such as Bill C-205. Surely, if the minister can set a precedent and, in effect, set up two Canadas economically, he can go to the Prime Minister and suggest that the Prime Minister be a little more flexible. I am not talking about a constitutional two Canadas, special status, associate status or deux nation. The good old Postmaster General can smile, Mr. Speaker. He may be smiling because he wished us all Christmas cheer and because there is to be a six-day delivery; thank God. But I suggest that so long as we legislators continue the sterile and puerile debate on semant c differences in respect of what we need in our constitution, we will be faced with the hard realities of provision such as we have in Bill C-205.
If there is any message which I would hope the minister would get from this debate, in view of all the apprehension I have about the principle of this bill, I would hope it would be to take the precedent which has been established by this bill to the constitutional discussions so that we could have some progress there.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE, LOAN GUARANTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating amendments to the Regional Development Incentives Act. In other days when Canada was not plagued with such serious economic difficulties, the minister seemed to have a much more realistic concept of what he hoped to accomplish with this act. In Halifax in October of 1968 the minister said the following about the purpose of the Regional Development Incentives Act:
So let me emphasize my first principle. It is that we will not offer short-run expediency or long-run vagueness. We want to have constructive, practical, medium-length plans. We are going to plan for every possible effort for 15 years.
At that time the minister was proposing a plan which would help the slow-growth areas of this country which are in need. It was obvious then, and it is even more obvious today, that in the ordinary run of events-I am thinking in terms of the market economy-the slow-growth areas would not and could not get the kind of industry and economic development which they require to use their raw materials and human resources.
Therefore, since one could not expect private industry to go into those slow-growth areas because it could do much better in the golden triangle of Toronto, Hamilton and Windsor and in the Montreal and Vancouver areas, the Maritimes, eastern Quebec, eastern Ontario and parts of Manitoba simply could not do without the kind of programs which were proposed under the Reginal Development Incentives Act. But now we have a different situation from that of October, 1968, when the minister made those remarks which I quoted. Today we are faced with major unemployment. There are almost 500,000 unemployed and by February, 1971, the figure will probably rise to 800,000. Almost 40 per cent of that figure, Mr. Speaker, is concentrated in the province of Quebec.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
When the minister suggests that members of this House from any party who criticize this bill and the proposals he is making, do so because they are anti-Quebec, he is not only being unfair but is doing a disservice to that province. I think it is fair to say that there is no Member of Parliament who does not realize that the problems of Quebec are so serious, with the unemployment and poverty there, that they must be solved. Unless they are solved, this country will not survive.

-do not need to object as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) is endeavouring to do. If he wants to speak, he can do so later. I do not think I have taken very much time and I do not need any

December 18, 1970
Regional Development Incentives Act lectures from him as to when I should speak, or for how long.
The problem of unemployment is of such importance that the country demands that major efforts be made. The expenditure of the $130 million which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) mentioned in his budget speech will not solve the problems of Canada or the unemployment problems of Quebec. The estimate of the department, which I think is too conservative, is that it costs $5,000 to provide one job under this program, so the total number of jobs we can expect to find is 26,000. Two months from now we will be faced with something like
200,000	people out of work. This unemployment is to a large extent due to the economic and fiscal programs adopted by the government on the advice of its top civil servants in the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance. The government decided that restraint was necessary so they put on the economic brakes and created unemployment. It is true that this year the increase in the cost of living has been lower than usual, but it has inevitably led to an increase in unemployment. The minister should have known that this would be a consequence in light of his background in the labour movement.
Having created unemployment on the one hand, on the other the government expects to meet some of the resultant problems with this program. But, Mr. Speaker, as I have already said, this bill and its proposals are too little and too late. In the department, in the legislation and in the administration there are very serious defects. The minister is probably the only person who knows anything about this department but he does not realize the difficulties. Some of the best people in the department, those who had the senior positions, have left. That is not an accident, Mr. Speaker. They left because the department and its programs have changed from being people-oriented, being concerned with the needs of the people they supposedly a'm to help, and have become almost entirely industry-oriented. I have talked to some of these people and I gather that they feel the department and the minister are now prepared to accept any type of growth, no matter whether it hurts the community concerned.
Let me illustrate briefly what I mean, Mr. Speaker. We have the ARDA and FRED programs, but what is their purpose? It is to rationalize the agricultural industry in the areas in which they aic oeing instituted and to consolidate farms into economic units. These are worthwhile and laudable objectives. But as far as I can see, no plans have been made to encourage farmers to leave the farm. Instead of being the rural poor, they will become the city pooi;, living on welfare. So far that is the only progress I can see as a result of the ARDA and FRED programs.
The department is providing incentives to industry but it does not seem to be concerned about how these are used. It certainly does not seem to be concerned about what type of employment is created. Under one of the earlier programs the government of Canada participated with the former government of Manitoba in the establishment of a pulp and paper industry at Le Pas-Churchill Forest Industries. I am not going into detail about how much was contributed in grants and subsidies and how little the owners, the believers in free enterprise, contributed of their own capital. But it is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that no provision was made by the department which put up the money, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, to apply pressure on the owners to employ the people who live in that area. There are virtually no Indians employed with Churchill Forest Industries at Le Pas. This is another valid criticism which can and must be made of the program which this government has devised.
Mr. Speaker, I was not a member of the committee but I had an opportunity to speak to some of the members of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council a few days ago.
I tell the minister that from them I got the impression that they could see no consistent, well thought-out program in the minister's statements or his answers to questions which would indicate that the government has any real plan on how to use the Regional Development Incentives Act.
As I said earlier, those who have criticized the present legislation support the idea that a special effort must be made to create more employment in the province of Quebec. But when the government and the minister bring in proposals which have the effect of making more than half the total land area of Canada eligible for assistance under a Regional Development Incentives Act, they destroy the whole point of an act designed to help slow-growth areas.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
If the minister is not concerned about the kind of comments, criticisms and suggestions made by people who appeared before the committee, people such as Professor Brewis, I do not know what one can do. Professor Brewis' comments about the program are so important and so crucial to any kind of success that it seems to me the minister is under an obligation to explain to the House where Professor Brewis was wrong, if he was wrong. I wish to quote a couple of paragraphs from the material Professor Brewis supplied to members of the House who were interested in his comments. He said:
The increase in the number of designated areas of one sort and another will almost certainly lead to action by provincial governments to include still other areas. The Saskatchewan government, for example, offers aid to firms outside the federally assisted areas. I suspect moreover that some provincial governments will become increasingly critical of federal policies of regional development.
Because we do not have a well thought-out federal plan which has been co-ordinated with the provinces, we are witnessing a kind of bargain basement sale. Every province, and certainly every have-not province, is busy with its own incentive plan. Each province bids against the others in the hope that industry will be encouraged to come to it and not to any other. I am thinking of the concessions made in Newfoundland. In particular, I am thinking of the oil refinery.
